question.text: What is the 'theta-gamma tradeoff' that applies to all option markets?

answer.text: Long options have positive gamma (favorable delta movement) but negative theta (time decay cost). Short options have negative gamma (adverse delta movement) but positive theta (time decay income). The tradeoff is: pay for gamma protection vs earn from time decay
Theta and gamma always move in the same direction
This tradeoff only applies to equity options, not currency or IR options
Theta-gamma tradeoff means you can only trade one Greek at a time

explanation.text: The Logic: A long option position has positive gamma (delta moves favourably as the underlying moves) but negative theta — the holder pays for this convexity through time decay. A short option position has the mirror profile: negative gamma (delta moves against the position as the underlying moves) but positive theta — the seller earns time decay as compensation for taking on the gamma risk. Long gamma and long theta cannot be combined; this opposition is the core "theta-gamma tradeoff". The Trap: Theta and gamma do not move in the same direction for a given position — they have opposite signs. The tradeoff is not confined to equity options, and it does not mean a trader can only trade one Greek at a time; rather, taking a view on one effectively commits the trader to the opposite sign on the other. Note: The NISM Series IV (Interest Rate Derivatives) workbook pages reviewed define theta and gamma and state that long option holders face negative theta while sellers earn positive theta, but the explicit "theta-gamma tradeoff" framing — with long/short gamma sign claims and a universal cross-market statement — was not located in the workbook pages reviewed. The framing above is presented as general option-Greeks industry knowledge rather than a workbook citation.
